sections.title: Instructional examples
sections.directions: This example shows how to justify a modelling choice.

items.prompt: Costs $5, pays $40 with probability 1/10. Expected value?

sections.title: Guided practice
sections.directions: Decide what the quantities are before you compute anything.

items.prompt: An insurer charges a premium of $12 and pays out $80 with probability 1/20. Find the insurer's expected profit per policy.
Option A has expected payoff $20 and Option B has expected payoff $5. On expected value alone, which should be chosen, and what does this criterion ignore?
choices: Option A; expected value ignores the spread of outcomes and the decider's tolerance for risk.
Option A; expected value already accounts for risk, so nothing is ignored.
Neither; expected value cannot compare two options.
Option B; expected value ignores the spread of outcomes and the decider's tolerance for risk.

items.prompt: Assess whether this is a fair decision mechanism: choosing between two people using a single fair coin flip.
choices: Fair; each person receives probability 2/6 = 1/3, so the assignment is equal.
Fair; each person has probability 1/2, and the mechanism gives neither an advantage.
Not fair; the three probabilities are 3/6, 2/6, and 1/6, which are unequal.
Fair, because any random device produces a fair decision.

sections.title: Extension and challenge
sections.directions: Plan in writing: what you will model, why that model, and how you will check it.

items.prompt: A game costs $21 to play. It pays $168 with probability 1/14 and nothing otherwise. Find the expected value to the player, and say whether the game is fair.
items.responseExpectation: Give the result and the reasoning that produced it. Show enough work that someone else could check each step.
